summary:
Checker of the lane "dev-loop". I ran the key measurements again on my own copies (the same source snapshot as the report, ports 4355 to 4357) and added four experiments that the report did not have. All my servers are stopped (`lsof -nP -iTCP:4351-4359 -sTCP:LISTEN` returns nothing). The shared server on port 4320 still runs. `git status --short` of the worktree is the same as at the start. No request went to visonaut.com. All my files are in /Users/diegohaz/.claude/jobs/f65a6229/tmp/perf/dev-loop/check/ (scripts, results/, logs/).

The machine was much busier than during the report: load average 60 to 580 (report: 8 to 100). So I compare counts, CPU time of the main thread (`Performance.enable` with `timeDomain: "threadTicks"`), and A/B runs in turns.

What holds (counted or measured again):
- All request and byte counts: preview 363 requests in development and 104 in production form; page explorer 586 and 175; gallery 16 documents, 4,883 to 4,897 and 1,358 to 1,371 requests; build 475,107 bytes; Tailwind scans 799 files and 18,534,173 bytes, 471 files are audit and docs.
- Main thread time of one document, within 15% of the report: preview 1,002 ms in development and 465 ms in production form; component explorer 2,261 and 1,728 ms.
- Share of style in production form: 34% (preview), 61% (3,617 elements), 35% (gallery).
- One saved .tsx file: 1 message, no reload, the complete style sheet again (617 KB), applied after 299 ms (234..887), n=5. With the gallery open: 16 messages, 16 downloads (8.7 MB), main thread 3,860 ms (2,323..5,516), style 2,072 ms, n=5.
- README.md and audit/content/findings.json reload the page in 5 of 5 runs each. With `@import "tailwindcss" source(".");` they send nothing in 5 of 5 runs, and the development sheet is 465,745 bytes.
- The real app: a .tsx change sends the CSS as a module (967 KB), no reload; CHANGELOG.md reloads the page in 5 of 5 runs.

What is wrong or not supported: 7 corrections (see the list). The two most important: (1) the report says that the development gallery waits for the network and that its main thread is busy for only 3.9 s. That is a read error: the main thread is busy for about 9.5 s, and 5.1 s of it is script. (2) The report says that the style cost does not depend on the size of the file. Half right: bytes do not matter, but rules that match no element still cost 24% to 43% of the style time.
verdict:
The report is right in its main direction and wrong in 3 points that change the answer. Accept it with the corrections below.

Right: the counts, the order "frames first" for the gallery, the Tailwind scan of audit and docs with its fix, the hot-update behavior, and "the plugin freshStyles is not a cause" (read in the source, not measured again).

Wrong: (1) the development gallery is limited by the main thread, not by the network; (2) "one document of the real app costs the same as one document of the lab" contradicts the report's own numbers (491 against 960 ms of main thread) and mine (484 against 901 ms CPU); (3) the claim that the style cost does not depend on the style sheet was not measured, and my experiment refutes half of it.

Incomplete: the cause "primitives" names no file and no mechanism. I give both below, as far as this lane can.

Not reproducible within the stated ranges because of the machine load (60 to 580): all wall times of the production form and of the gallery, and the cold start. I do not call them wrong: the ratios hold.
directAnswer:
Is the belief "it is the huge generated CSS" right? PARTLY RIGHT.

1. The size in bytes is not the problem (measured). I loaded the same production page with a sheet of double size (940 KB, the second half has rules for classes that no element has). Style time: 167 ms against 159 ms for 647 elements, and 684 against 744 ms for 3,617 elements. No change outside the range. Parse and download are a few ms.

2. What the browser does with the rules is a large part of each page (measured, CPU time, n=7, in turns):

| Sheet | Bytes | Style ms, 647 elements | Style ms, 3,617 elements | Main thread ms |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| full | 475,107 | 159 (126..172) | 744 (574..977) | 440 / 1,268 |
| only rules that match an element | 169,761 / 200,282 | 121 (95..138) | 425 (367..564) | 407 / 924 |
| double | 939,689 | 167 (150..194) | 684 (617..1126) | 459 / 1,165 |
| no CSS | 0 | 5 | 8 | 256 / 364 |

So the CSS causes 42% of the main thread time of the settled review page and 71% of the page with 3,617 elements. Rules that match nothing still cost 24% to 43% of the style time, because Chrome must test them against each element. The page with the reduced sheet has the same computed styles (0 of 546 elements differ) and the same screenshot.

3. But this cost is not why the lab feels "extremely slow". One settled page needs 0.4 to 0.8 s in production form. The lab multiplies that base cost:
- by the frames: the gallery is 16 full apps. With the frame documents blocked, the gallery is usable after 1.07 s in development and 0.48 s in production form (measured, n=5). With frames, in this session: 18.6 s and 10.0 s. So 94% of the wait is the frames.
- by the development server: 2.2 times the main thread time for one document (1,002 against 465 ms), 3.4 times the script time (675 against 201 ms), 363 requests against 104.
- by this machine: the same production page needed 0.4 s at a load average of 22 to 47 (report) and 0.5 to 2.2 s at 150 to 580 (my runs).
- by the edits of other agents: each saved file makes each open document download the complete sheet and calculate all styles again (gallery: 2.3 to 5.5 s of blocked main thread for one save).

"Are you doing something unnecessary, or is it the primitives?" Both.
- The lab does two things that it does not need: live frames in the gallery cards, and a Tailwind scan of apps/lab/audit and apps/lab/docs (9.4% of the built CSS, 475,107 to 430,507 bytes, and a full page reload for each edit of a Markdown or JSON file there).
- The primitives set the base cost: about 0.21 to 0.25 ms of style for each element at each full style calculation. Typical pages need much less. The real app has the same primitives.

For the real app: it is one document, so the largest factor does not exist there. The base cost stays and grows with the element count.

corrections.claim: Fact: "The gallery needs 9.3 s in development although its main thread is busy for 3.9 s, because 16 documents wait for 4,814 requests on one Node process and 6 connections." Table 5.1: gallery dev main thread 3,932 ms, script 1,446 ms.
corrections.problem: Read error in measure-load.mjs. The counters are read 1 s after the last request ends. In the report's own run 1 the last request ended at 3,756 ms, but the frames hydrated until 7,808 ms (node frame-timeline.mjs on results/lab-dev-vs-prod.json). So the counters missed about half of the work. The report's own trace says 9,589 ms of main thread and 5,543 ms of script for the same load (notes.md section 7). My rerun, where the requests ended later: main thread 9,534 ms (9,085..12,045), script 5,053 ms, style 2,282 ms, n=5. The server wait was 1 ms median for each request (node gallery-network.mjs).
corrections.fix: Replace the fact: the development gallery is limited by the main thread. About 9.5 s of main thread for 16 documents: 53% script (unbundled development modules and the development build of React, 16 times), 24% style. Production form: 5,430 ms (4,506..5,529), script 1,342, style 1,877. Remove the assumption about the 6 connections. The numbers "gallery 1238 of 3932 ms (31%)" and "1507 of 3635 ms (41%)" must be read with the same doubt: my shares are 24% (development) and 35% (production form).

corrections.claim: "The same path is as slow in the real app. One document of the real app costs the same as one document of the lab."
corrections.problem: The report's own table says the opposite for the main thread: web /runs/<id> 491 ms, lab review preview 960 ms. Its "usable" medians (1,675 and 1,621 ms) have ranges of 677..2,503 and 1,558..3,254, so they cannot show equality. My rerun, in turns, n=5, load 94 to 157: web /runs/<id> 246 requests, usable 797 ms (603..3,101), main thread CPU 484 ms, script 273, style 128, 429 elements. Lab review preview: 363 requests, usable 1,880 ms (1,675..2,270), main thread CPU 901 ms, script 596, style 172, 559 elements.
corrections.fix: Say: the development path is the same kind (unbundled modules, the same three large pre-bundled files, the same CSS behavior), but the settled review page of the lab costs about 1.9 times the main thread time of the current review page of the real app in development, mostly script (596 against 273 ms). So expect the real app in development to get slower when the settled design is implemented, by about that factor for this page (estimate from one page pair).

corrections.claim: Cause "primitives": "It grows with the number of elements, not with the size of the file." And: "The size of the CSS in bytes is not the problem."
corrections.problem: The report did not test a smaller or a larger sheet. I did (css-ab2.mjs, production form, CPU time, n=7, in turns). Bytes: right, a doubled sheet changes nothing. But rules that match no element are not free: with only the matching rules (712 or 868 of 3,027 style rules), style time is 121 against 159 ms (-24%) for 647 elements and 425 against 744 ms (-43%; -33% against the control that is written from the CSSOM, 632 ms) for 3,617 elements. Main thread: -7.5% and -27%. The reduced sheet draws the same page (css-validate.mjs: 0 of 546 elements differ, screenshots are byte-equal).
corrections.fix: Say: the cost grows with elements times the rules that Chrome must test or apply for each element. File bytes do not matter. Rules for classes that no element has do not matter. Rules that Chrome tests against every element matter, also when they match nothing. Note the limit of the experiment: "match no element at load" also removes hover, focus, and disabled rules, which a real page needs. So 24% to 43% is the upper limit of what a smaller sheet can give.

corrections.claim: Cause "primitives": no file and no mechanism ("the lanes for the CSS and for the runtime have the analysis").
corrections.problem: The task asks for the exact file and mechanism when a cause is in the copied primitives or in @ariakit/tailwind.
corrections.fix: Add what I measured with the selector statistics of Chrome (selector-stats.mjs, production form, page with 3,617 elements): 2.4 million match attempts, 244,307 matches; each element is styled about 3 times in one load (10,223 element recalculations). Selector matching is the smaller part: 180 ms of 1,249 ms of style recalculation (with trace overhead). Mechanism 1 (documented and counted): recipes of the copied primitives give selectors without a class in the last part, so Chrome tests them against every element: 18,835 attempts and 0 matches each. Sources: apps/lab/src/components/ariakit/styles/control.ts lines 176 to 184 (`[*:has(+&)]:me-[...]`), input.ts lines 31 and 32 (`**:ui-disabled:cursor-not-allowed`, `ui-field-disabled:**:ak-ink-0`), choice.ts lines 134 and 195 (`ui-disabled-within:**:ak-ink-0`). apps/web has the same in control.ts lines 146 to 154. Mechanism 2 (counted; its time share is an assumption): the rules that match are expensive to apply. `.ak-layer` matched 17,352 times. The built sheet has 374 `@container` blocks, 780 `style(` queries, 247 `@property` rules, 2,622 custom property declarations, and 4,731 `var(` uses. They come from apps/lab/node_modules/@ariakit/tailwind/src/output.css (98,876 bytes, 78 `@container style(...)` blocks, `@utility ak-layer` at line 118). The split of mechanism 2 is the work of the CSS lane.

corrections.claim: Real app: "apps/web/src/styles.css: scan only the source folder" with `@import "tailwindcss" source(".");`. And for the lab: sheet 517,488 to 465,745 bytes.
corrections.problem: Wrong file for the real app: apps/web/src/styles.css has only `@import "./review.css";`. The Tailwind import is in apps/web/src/review.css line 1. The gain there is small: 78 of 272 scanned files are outside src (tooling 39, migrations 33), 9,071 candidates against 7,969 (node count-scan-repo.mjs web). For the lab, two facts are missing: the change needs a restart of the development server (measured: the running server still served 517,968 bytes after the edit, and 465,745 bytes after a restart), and the production build also gets smaller: 475,107 to 430,507 bytes (-9.4%), `style(` queries 780 to 464.

corrections.claim: Fix for the frames: "Expected: the gallery is usable in under 1 s in development (estimate)" and "about 214 requests"; smaller step `{ rootMargin: "0px" }`, "fewer frames load (not measured)".
corrections.problem: Both can be measured. With the frame documents blocked (measure-load.mjs --block=/preview/, n=5, load 113 to 146): gallery usable 1,068 ms (921..1,262) in development with 259 requests, and 475 ms (305..582) in production form with 107 requests. The directions page: 1,057 ms and 707 ms. For the margin (count-frames.mjs): at 1440 by 900, 9 of the 15 loaded frames are in the viewport; at 600, 5 of 11; at 300, 4 of 5. In the current lab on the shared server (round 3) the gallery has 10 frames and is 1,133 px high, so all 10 are in the viewport at 1440 by 900: the smaller step gives nothing there. It also makes each frame load again at each scroll, because useNearViewport removes a frame that is not near (apps/lab/src/lab/ui/preview-frame.tsx lines 41 to 57 and 204).
corrections.fix: Keep "pictures in place of live frames" with the measured gain: 16 to 20 times less wait for the gallery in this session. Drop the `rootMargin` step as a fix for the current lab. Name what pictures break: the theme toggle and the look controls no longer change the cards live, and the pictures are old after each edit until the script runs again.

corrections.claim: All wall times of the report: preview in production form 397 ms (360..407); gallery 9.3 s in development and 3.7 s in production form; server start 2.8 s; first document after a start 2.8 s wait and 4.8 s usable.
corrections.problem: Not reproducible within the stated ranges on this machine now. Mine, load average 60 to 580: preview in production form 758 ms (533..2,180); gallery 18.6 s (12.7..23.5) in development and 10.0 s (6.9..13.1) in production form; server start 6.0 s (n=1) and 10.3 s (n=1, two servers started together); first document after a start 14.2 s wait and 21.0 s usable (n=1). The ratios hold: development against production form 2.6 times for the preview (report 3.8), 1.9 times for the gallery (report 2.5).
corrections.fix: Give each wall time with its load average and say that it scales with the load by a factor of 2 to 5. Use the main thread numbers and the counts as the stable facts. The preview in development (1,997 ms, 1,382..6,097) is inside the report's range.

causes.cause: The lab shows each design in a live frame, and each frame is a full app: document, style sheet, fonts, React, router, module graph, and a full style calculation. The gallery loads all its frames at once (15 in the measured snapshot, 10 in the lab of round 3). The compare view, the directions page, and the page explorer have 3, 6, and 1 frames. Source: apps/lab/src/lab/ui/surface-card.tsx line 85 and apps/lab/src/lab/ui/preview-frame.tsx.

causes.cause: The development path of the tool stack (Vite without bundling, the Cloudflare plugin with workerd, TanStack Start, Tailwind). Each document loads 290 to 363 files and runs development builds. Tailwind registers each scanned file as a dependency of the style sheet (`addWatchFile` in @tailwindcss/vite/dist/index.mjs, version 4.3.3), so each saved source file sends the complete CSS again, and the document calculates all its styles again. The plugin keeps found class names in a set that it never empties, so a long-running server only grows its sheet.

Measured on a copy of apps/web: 226 to 246 requests for one document; a saved .tsx file sends the CSS as a module (967 KB) and applies after 913 ms (328..2,639) at load 155 to 193; the first document after a server start needed 5.4 s of wait and 11.8 s to usable (n=1, load 125).

causes.cause: The Ariakit UI primitives: the copied recipes in src/components/ariakit/styles and the package @ariakit/tailwind. Two mechanisms. (1) Recipe classes such as `[*:has(+&)]:me-[...]` (control.ts lines 176 to 184), `**:ui-disabled:cursor-not-allowed` and `ui-field-disabled:**:ak-ink-0` (input.ts lines 31 and 32), `ui-disabled-within:**:ak-ink-0` (choice.ts lines 134 and 195) give selectors that Chrome tests against every element. (2) The rules that match (`.ak-layer`, `.ak-frame`, `.ak-text` from @ariakit/tailwind/src/output.css) set many custom properties and use container style queries, and each element is styled about 3 times in one load.

That is 0.21 to 0.25 ms for each element. With no CSS the same pages need 256 and 364 ms, so the CSS causes 42% and 71% of the main thread time. So it reads apps/lab/audit, apps/lab/docs, and README.md. Class names in that text become rules. A change of a scanned file that is not JavaScript or CSS sends `full-reload` to each open document (the `hotUpdate` hook of the plugin).

realApp:
What follows for apps/web when the settled design is implemented there:

1. It will not be "extremely slow" as the lab is. The largest factor in the lab is the frames (16 full apps on one page, 94% of the gallery wait). The real app is one document. The settled review page as one document in production form: 440 ms of main thread CPU, usable after 0.4 s at a load average of 22 to 47 (report) and 0.5 to 2.2 s at 150 to 580 (my runs). No compression and no network are in these numbers.

2. It will be slower than the real app is today, in development (estimate from one page pair, measured in turns): the settled review page needs 901 ms of main thread CPU against 484 ms for the current review page of apps/web, 363 requests against 246, and it was usable after 1,880 ms against 797 ms. The difference is mostly script (596 against 273 ms). The report's sentence "costs the same" is wrong.

3. The CSS cost of the primitives comes with the design, in production too. Measured: 0.21 to 0.25 ms of style for each element at each full style calculation; 36% of the main thread time of the review page; 59% for a page with 3,617 elements (744 ms). A full calculation happens at the load, at a theme change, and at each hot CSS update in development. So keep the element count of a page low (render long lists in parts). A smaller sheet can remove at most 24% to 43% of that style time (measured limit); the rest is the cost of the rules that apply, and that needs a change in the recipes or in @ariakit/tailwind.

4. Development loop: each saved file sends the complete CSS (967 KB as a module in apps/web) and starts a full style calculation. For one document that is about 0.2 s of main thread on this machine (measured: 170 to 470 ms). It grows with the element count of the open page.

5. Small things to take over:
```css
/* apps/web/src/review.css, line 1 (not styles.css) */
@import "tailwindcss" source(".");
```
It stops the full reload for CHANGELOG.md, migrations, and tooling files (measured: 5 of 5 reloads now). The CSS gain there is small (9,071 to 7,969 candidates). And restart a development server that has run for days.

6. Not measured: apps/web in production form with the new design, a real network, compression, and a page of the real app with more than 429 elements.
remainingDoubts: Machine load. My runs had a load average of 60 to 580. No wall time of mine is a fact about a quiet machine. I used CPU time of the main thread where I could, but CPU time also grows under such load (cache and core sharing): the range of one variant was up to 1.7 times.

The experiment with the reduced sheet removes every rule that matches no element after the load. That includes hover, focus, and disabled rules, which a real page needs. So 24% to 43% is an upper limit, not an expected gain. I did not test a sheet without only the rules from audit and docs, and not a sheet without only the selectors that Chrome tests against every element.

Why the rules that match are expensive (custom properties, container style queries, 3 style passes for each element) is counted but not split by time. The time share of `@container style()` is an assumption. This is the work of the CSS lane.

The "double" sheet doubles only rules whose selectors have a class. Rules without a class are in it two times with the same selector. So it shows that bytes and rules for other classes are free, not that every added rule is free.

The frames-blocked numbers and the with-frames numbers come from two runs 15 minutes apart at different loads (113 to 146 against 150 to 580). The factor of 16 to 20 is therefore rough. The report's with-frames numbers at lower load (9.3 s and 3.7 s) give a factor of about 8.

I did not measure again: the scenario switch and theme toggle (check-switch.mjs), the cold start cycle with n=5, the plugin freshStyles with and without (I only read its source: it invalidates the same module that Tailwind already watches), and the Tailwind timing of apps/web.

The report's other counters that are read 1 s after the last request (page explorer, compare view, directions page) can have the same read error as the gallery. My page explorer number in development is 35% higher than the report's (1,944 against 1,442 ms).

The 614 KB sheet of the shared server: the mechanism is documented and I measured it in the small (10 probe classes stayed until a restart). That the complete 97 KB difference is old classes is still an assumption. I did not restart the shared server.

I measured the lab snapshot of round 2 (15 gallery cards), as the report did. The lab of round 3 has 10 gallery frames (counted on the shared server). I did not load its gallery with frames on the shared server.

Headless Chrome only. Not the maintainer's browser, its extensions, its DevTools, or its open tabs. An open DevTools window makes style calculation much slower (my trace with selector statistics: 2,762 ms of style against 744 ms without).

One known fault of my own first attempt: Chrome's CSS rule usage (CSS.startRuleUsageTracking) reports the complete `@layer utilities` block as one used range for this sheet, so that result is not valid (results/css-ab-first-try-used-not-valid.json). The second form (css-ab2.mjs) finds the used rules in the page. Its built-in computed-style check was also faulty; css-validate.mjs is the valid check.
